item.title: Public interest at heart of CPC self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Public interest at heart of CPC self-governance Maintaining Party's fundamental bond with the people seen as key to leadership Before leaving a budget hotel in Fuping county, Hebei province, on Dec 29, 2012, Xi Jinping instructed his staff to make sure the dinner bill was paid, recalled Jia Chunhong, the hotel's catering manager. The meal itself was simple: four homestyle dishes, soup, some staple foods, and no alcohol served. The two-day field trip to Fuping county came just six weeks after Xi was elected general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee. Only 25 days before the dinner, Xi had chaired a meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that adopted the eight-point decision on improving work conduct and maintaining close ties with the people, setting out requirements for officials on matters ranging from grassroots research to meetings and official receptions. At that meeting, Xi said, "Only when we are under pressure and supervision can people enjoy a more comfortable and satisfying life and have a higher opinion of us." The eight-point decision became an early step in the CPC's broader drive to exercise full and rigorous self-governance, extending strict requirements in areas ranging from officials' conduct to Party building as a whole. At a gathering marking the CPC's 95th anniversary in July 2016, Xi warned that the Party could eventually lose its qualifications to govern if it failed to enforce strict self-governance and address serious internal problems that drew strong public complaints. In the same speech, Xi described standing with the people as the Party's fundamental political position, saying that the people's support, approval, satisfaction and consent should serve as the fundamental criteria for evaluating its work. For Xi, the Party must always guard against and correct with resolve the practices the people oppose and resent. "We will focus on enhancing the Party's capacity for long-term governance, preserving its advanced nature and integrity, and maintaining its close bond with the people," he said while addressing a gathering marking the CPC's 105th anniversary in July this year. Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at Tsinghua University's National Institute of Strategic Studies, said that full and rigorous Party self-governance was not simply about enforcing discipline, but about preserving the CPC's fundamental bond with the people. "Public oversight and the Party's self-reform reinforce each other. Both are essential to ensuring that power is exercised in the public interest and that officials remain committed to serving the people," he said. Ultimately, the effectiveness of Party building should be measured by whether it strengthens public trust, protects the people's interests and keeps the Party closely connected with those it serves, Xie said. Former Ethiopian president Mulatu Teshome said the CPC's internal rules and discipline have made the Party "stronger and stronger", helping sustain its leadership and maintain policy continuity in China's development. He said that corruption could drive a wedge between a governing party and the people it served, eroding public trust and undermining national development. Teshome stressed that misconduct by officials should not be tolerated and that maintaining close ties with the people is essential to effective governance. Concrete benefits Gulnar Shaimergenova, director of the China Studies Center in Kazakhstan, said stricter Party governance should translate into better-performing institutions and concrete benefits for the public. "Full and rigorous Party self-governance goes beyond combating corruption. It is also about improving the way institutions function, ensuring that officials fulfill their responsibilities and that government policies produce tangible benefits for the people," she said. She pointed to the CPC's eight-point decision as an effort to tackle formalism and bureaucratic inefficiency, allowing officials to devote more time to employment, public services and other everyday concerns, rather than unnecessary paperwork and procedural formalities. Beyond improving work practices, Shaimergenova said the real test is whether officials can deliver lasting improvements in people's lives. "Effective administration should not be measured simply by economic indicators or the number of policies introduced, but by whether development produces sustainable improvements in people's well-being," she said. That emphasis also underpins this year's Party-wide education campaign on establishing and practicing a correct view of governance performance, which shows China's unequivocal philosophy — governance is for the people. "Ultimately, I believe the people-first principle becomes meaningful when it is reflected not only in strategic documents, but also in the everyday conduct of officials and in improvements that citizens can genuinely experience," she said. Tongan Deputy Prime Minister Viliami Uasike Latu said the CPC's internal governance mechanisms help hold individual members accountable for their conduct and ensure that they fulfill their responsibilities. Having visited China more than five times, Latu said he was impressed by the emphasis that Chinese leaders have placed on listening to public concerns and remaining accountable to the people. Nigerian lawmaker Satomi Alhaji Ahmad said that clean governance requires leaders to put their people's interests ahead of their own. "They put the country first," he said, praising what he saw as Chinese leaders' commitment to serving the public, rather than pursuing personal interests. He also stressed that ordinary people should benefit from good governance through better access to education, healthcare and other essential services. That concern for public interest is also reflected in efforts to tackle corruption and misconduct at the grassroots level. Since 2024, China's top disciplinary and supervisory authorities have led a nationwide campaign targeting misconduct and corruption that directly affect people's livelihoods. Figures reported in October showed that since the campaign began, authorities nationwide had investigated and dealt with 2.253 million instances of misconduct and corruption affecting the public and disciplined 1.555 million people. Disciplinary and supervisory bodies had also helped resolve 6.98 million pressing problems affecting the public, in areas including education, healthcare and other essential services. Noticeable change Former British lawmaker Mark Logan, who has followed China's development for about two decades, said he has witnessed a marked change in the country's approach to corruption. "You can definitely say today that China has much less corruption," he said. "There's a real focus on delivering for people," he added.

item.title: Robots wow travelers over weeklong holiday
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Robots wow travelers over weeklong holiday Robots poured tea, played table tennis and answered children's questions about marine animals at a theme park in South China during this year's National Day holiday from Oct 1 to 7. Elsewhere, machines served coffee and ice cream, helped tourists scale mountains and prepared millions of meals. The holiday rush gave China's robotics manufacturers an opportunity to introduce their machines "face to face" with consumers, as tourist attractions, retailers and restaurants explored new ways to draw visitors and enhance services. At Chimelong Spaceship Park in Hengqin, Guangdong province, more than 300 robots developed by Shanghai-based AgiBot were deployed across over 100 interactive locations, welcoming visitors and providing guided tours, science education and entertainment. "I didn't expect robots to pour tea or play table tennis," said Li Linlin, who was visiting from Guangzhou, Guangdong, with her two sons. "We originally came to see the spaceship-themed attractions and marine animals, but the two boys were most fascinated by the robots that could chat and play with them." The deployment, which began in September, forms part of a 10-year strategic partnership between AgiBot and Chimelong Group. Rather than renting machines for holiday performances, the park purchased them for permanent use, allowing the partners to develop new attractions and refine the technology through daily interactions with visitors. "Technology is fast becoming a new tourism draw for China," said Wu Liyun, a professor at the China Academy of Culture and Tourism at Beijing International Studies University, adding that foreign visitors increasingly seek to experience how smart technologies are being integrated into everyday life. The growing interest is opening commercial opportunities for China's robotics industry, particularly in tourism, retail and other consumer services. An estimate based on publicly announced projects suggests that nearly 30 robotics firms had entered these sectors, with thousands of humanoid and other embodied robots in use during the weeklong holiday. Such applications are also a focus of China's broader push to use technology to expand spending on services. Guidelines released by the Ministry of Commerce and eight other departments on Oct 19 called for wider commercial applications of embodied artificial intelligence, as well as new cultural and tourism products and smart services using AI and other technologies. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism has selected 14 projects to pilot AI applications in the sector, aiming to develop approaches that can be adopted nationwide, Zhou Hanping, an official with the ministry's industrial development department, said at a news conference on the policy. For robot manufacturers, daily use at tourist attractions provides a practical test of both technical performance and consumer appeal. Wang Chuang, senior vice-president at AgiBot, told Xinhua Finance that simple games such as rock-paper-scissors and table tennis had attracted greater visitor interest than some technically demanding demonstrations. The company therefore plans to adjust the activities regularly based on visitor feedback and usage data. AgiBot also aims to make its robots less dependent on human supervision. Xiong Yan, co-president of AgiBot, said the park initially needed roughly one staff member for every three robots, although staffing requirements varied by specialized tasks performed. The company aims to reduce that requirement to one employee for every 10 robots, and eventually one for every 20, through improved automation and operational management. Reducing supervision and maintenance costs could make large-scale deployments more commercially feasible. Other manufacturers are expanding into retail. Chinese robotics maker Galbot has introduced more than 200 automated retail stations at locations including Beijing's Summer Palace, West Lake in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, and Gulangyu Island in Xiamen, Fujian province. Robots at the stations handle customer orders and product deliveries. Wearable exoskeleton robots are serving a different need — helping tourists walk longer distances with less physical effort at destinations including Taishan Mountain in Shandong province and Xi'an's ancient city wall in Shaanxi province. Beyond tourist attractions, specialized robots are already performing high-volume tasks hidden from customer view in restaurant kitchens, where efficiency and consistency matter more than entertainment. Chinese cooking robot manufacturer Xianglu Robotics said 12,741 of its automated cooking machines were working across 334 cities during the holiday, completing nearly 6 million stir-frying tasks. The company estimates that the output was enough to serve approximately 18 million diners, based on an average of three people per cooking cycle. In a written response to China Daily, Xianglu said the cooking figures were collected through its operating data platform, while batch sizes ranged from meals for individual restaurant customers to larger quantities used in institutional catering. It said cooking volumes had risen year-on-year, largely because more machines had been installed, although it did not provide comparable per-machine utilization figures. The wider commercial potential of robots in tourism is still being tested. Liang Zengxian, a tourism professor at Sun Yat-sen University, told Southern Finance that robots could complement rather than replace human performers, providing new forms of interaction and entertainment. Liang said integrating robotics with tourism could bring measurable economic benefits, although more real-world applications would be needed to fully demonstrate their commercial value.

item.title: Shanghai indices begin updated rules
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Shanghai indices begin updated rules Expert: 15% cap can keep a behemoth from 'kidnapping' overall market The latest compilation adjustments to the major indices on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, which took effect on Monday, will help further cushion market volatility and lower risks, which is of great importance at a time of global downward pressure, said experts. Two major changes have been implemented, according to the latest revision details announced in late September. First, a constituent's weight is now capped at 15 percent. Second, the timing for removing risk-warning counters from the indices has been moved earlier. Previously, a stock was taken from the index on the first trading day after the second Friday of the month following the date the risk warning took effect. Now it is dropped on the first trading day after the second Friday of the month following the date the risk warning was issued. Tian Lihui, a finance professor at Nankai University, compares the two practices to a "flow-control valve" and "filter" for the indices. The 15-percent cap can prevent one behemoth company from "kidnapping" the overall market performance due to its huge size. Bringing the removal date forward ushers disqualified counters out of the sample pool more efficiently. "Amid higher downward pressure, the market is more sensitive to any factors that might aggravate fluctuations. The latest adjustments can cleanse the index ecosystem at the algorithmic level, ensuring the indices objectively and fairly reflect overall quality even in a weak market," Tian said. Four major indices — including the SSE Composite Index and the STAR Composite Index — are subject to the 15-percent cap limit. Guo Shiliang, an independent financial commentator, said the new rule is mainly an adjustment to the compilation rules of the SSE series of indices rather than a cap applied uniformly on all A-share market indices. Given that the SSE Composite Index's weight composition is relatively balanced and the weight of any single heavyweight stock is far below the 15-percent cap, the impact on the SSE Composite Index's constituent shares is fairly limited, and the room for subsequent constituent weight adjustments will be relatively small. By contrast, the impact on weight adjustments for the tech-focused STAR Composite Index's constituent stocks will be larger. "Take memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies as an example. Prior to the new rule, the company's market-cap weight would have exceeded 20 percent once formally added to the STAR Composite Index, well above the 15-percent cap. The new rule will effectively reduce the index's overreliance on any single stock," Guo said. As for the adjustment to risk-warning stocks, Yang Delong, chief economist at First Seafront Fund, said that the liquidity of these companies may deteriorate in a weak market. Bringing the removal date forward helps shorten the time that passive products are stuck holding problem stocks and reduces the impact costs of concentrated rebalancing, thereby protecting the interests of investors holding funds that track the index, Yang said. This move represents another major adjustment in SSE indices since July 2020, when special treatment stocks — those with abnormal financial or operational situations — were removed from the sample pool and the inclusion of new stocks was delayed. Analysts from Guosen Securities said that the indices' long-term representation and investability are likely to steadily improve after the latest changes. Wu Xinkun, chief strategist at Guosen Securities, admitted there is short-term downward pressure on the A-share market, which is a combined result of external and internal factors. Rising oil prices amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East — as well as the high inflation and interest rates in the United States — have suppressed the pricing of risky assets globally. In the domestic market, investor sentiment for the tech sector has not bottomed out while the market is still awaiting more capital inflows. The market fluctuation is thus magnified, Wu said. But the outlook on the A-share market's mid- to long-term performance is by no means pessimistic. Companies' profitability is improving, and more long-term capital will be ushered into A shares, providing support for a rebound likely to take place this quarter, he added. shijing@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Long March's grit, resolve lauded
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Long March's grit, resolve lauded Red Army's achievements could inspire people around the world, diplomats say The leadership of the Communist Party of China, support of the people and unwavering resolve enabled the Red Army to overcome overwhelming odds on the Long March, laying the foundations for modern China, foreign diplomats said on Monday, as they called for the same determination to address today's global challenges. Diplomats and envoys from 106 embassies and five international organizations in China toured The Great Expedition, an exhibition at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution in Beijing that commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March. The Long March was a strategic military maneuver carried out by the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army of the CPC from 1934 to 1936. The troops crossed rivers, mountains and grasslands to break the siege by the Chinese Kuomintang forces. Somphone Sichaleune, the Lao ambassador to China, identified the CPC leadership, the solidarity of the Chinese people and their support for the Red Army as crucial to the victory. He said history provided a "vivid example for the new generation", adding that understanding it matters as people embark on new journeys to build their country, while its significance extended to people elsewhere pursuing national liberation and progress. Stephen Jackson, the United Nations' resident coordinator in China, highlighted a "sense of determination and the ability to take the long view", linking these qualities to China's long history of overcoming challenges. He described the two-year Long March as an extraordinary feat of determination and endurance. "We need that kind of determination in the world. And China is showing it," he said, calling for renewed commitment to multilateralism, international cooperation and a shared future for humanity. Hussam Al Husseini, the Jordanian ambassador to China, said that witnessing China's current development has deepened his appreciation for the sacrifices made during the Long March and the resilience and determination of the Chinese people that helped lay the foundations of modern China. "Many of the sacrifices we don't understand until later," he said. He described the march as "an amazing story of determination" and resolve, noting that despite the severe hardships they faced, the Chinese people maintained clear goals. Hodan Osman Abdi, the Somali ambassador to China, said that she had learned about the Long March mainly from books. Tracing the route of the march at the exhibition and learning about its pivotal moments gave her a deeper understanding of the distance traveled and the hardships overcome. "I believe it really showed the Chinese people and different generations what they can achieve with perseverance and hard work, despite the odds," she said. The achievements of the Red Army amid scarce resources could inspire people worldwide, Abdi added. Luamanuvae Albert Mariner, the Samoan ambassador to China, said the exhibition highlighted "the values of perseverance, determination and courage" that continue to influence China's leadership. In his welcoming address to the diplomats, Hong Lei, China's assistant foreign minister, said the Long March spirit was a shared asset of world civilizations, with its values reflecting aspirations for truth, justice and peace. China is ready to work with other countries for peace and development, he added. zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn

LONDON -- Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or award on Monday, becoming England's first winner in 25 years. item.title: From building machines to building lives
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Tianjin is a city that was born of a river and prospers by the sea. Join China Daily reporter Yan Dongjie and host Erik Nilsson to see how Tianjin's old factory buildings are being reintegrated into everyday city life. In Hedong District, Jinyi Park was once the birthplace of New China's first fully geared lathe. Today, this former machine tool factory is a vibrant slow-life leisure hub for young people, where coffee replaces machine oil and old workshops host performances. Next, visit the yarn-dyed fabric factory in Xiqing District, where 35 old factory buildings have been preserved and turned into a 24-hour commercial area. As night falls, BBQ, hotpot and specially brewed craft beer bring the old factory back to life. The revitalization has filled the gap in Tianjin's night economy and helped the city top China's most livable list for two consecutive years.

item.title: Chinese opera hits big in small theaters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Tradition turns intimate as audiences get a close-up look at how various styles are created, performed, and expressed, Chen Nan reports. Li Chanchan and Fan Yuyan, two young students from the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts in Beijing, drew a crowd in a courtyard as they demonstrated a traditional jaw-dropping feat before one unleashed a burst of fire. The flames flared and vanished in an instant, prompting gasps and applause from spectators gathered among the courtyard's gray bricks and tiled roofs. The demonstration is a signature Qinqiang Opera stage skill: fire-breathing, known for its dramatic visual impact. Other performers demonstrated the sweeping spear movements of Peking Opera, offering a glimpse of the physical precision and theatrical spectacle that has sustained traditional Chinese opera for generations. At the 13th Xiqu Opera Black Box Festival, which opened at Star Theaters in Beijing on Oct 14, tradition is also being explored through more intimate, unexpected storytelling forms. The festival runs through Nov 22 and brings together 16 productions tailored for smaller theaters spanning 11 traditional Chinese opera genres, including Peking Opera, Kunqu Opera, Yuju Opera, Pingju Opera, and Cantonese Opera. The opening performance, The Face in the Mirror, a Huaiju Opera production, takes audiences into a world of illusion and psychological unease, asking what happens when people finally obtain what they desire.

item.title: World Bank director sees China's buzzwords
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
World Bank country director: What development keywords can a robot exhibition reveal about China? Over the past four plus decades and more, China has achieved rapid development and structural transformation, lifting 800 million people out of extreme poverty, and steadily raising incomes and welfare. Citing the World Robot Conference in Beijing as an example, Tatiana Rosito, World Bank country director for China, Mongolia, and Korea, noted that robotics is accelerating on the ground in China, boosting productivity and changing people's daily lives. She said she looks forward to China's 15th Five-Year Plan, including new productive forces, high-quality development, more and better jobs, and green transition. The World Bank's cooperation with China will focus on three pillars: promoting productivity and job growth, enhancing human capital for better jobs, and strengthening resilient infrastructure and natural capital. (Reporter: Li Wei; Video: Pan Yixuan, Cheng Zixin)
